title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problemStatement:
Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s.

A string is palindromic if it reads the same forward and backward.
constraints: s consist of only digits and English letters

solutions.detailedExplanation: This brute force solution exhaustively checks all possible substrings. The outer two loops generate every substring by varying start index i and end index j. For each substring s[i:j+1], we use two pointers to check if it's a palindrome: start l at i and r at j, then move them toward each other while the characters match. If l >= r (pointers meet or cross), the substring is a palindrome. We track the longest palindrome found so far by comparing lengths. The time complexity is O(n³) because we have O(n²) substrings and checking each one takes O(n) time. The space complexity is O(n) for storing the result string.

Not updating both res and resLen when finding longer palindrome
Comparing lengths incorrectly (should use j - i + 1, not j - i)
Starting inner loop at 0 instead of i (generates duplicate work)
solutions.whyItWorks: The algorithm correctly identifies palindromes by checking if characters at symmetric positions match. The two-pointer palindrome check works because if s[l] == s[r] for all pairs moving inward, the substring must read the same forwards and backwards. By checking all substrings, we're guaranteed to find the longest palindrome. The condition l >= r ensures we've checked all character pairs (when l > r, all pairs matched; when l == r, we have odd-length palindrome with middle character).
keyInsights: Brute force: check all O(n²) substrings
Two-pointer technique verifies palindrome in O(n) time
Condition l >= r confirms palindrome (pointers met or crossed)
Track both result string and length to avoid redundant length calculations
Cubic time complexity makes this impractical for large inputs

solutions.detailedExplanation: This DP solution builds a table where dp[i][j] represents whether substring s[i:j+1] is a palindrome. The key insight is that a substring is a palindrome if: (1) its outer characters match (s[i] == s[j]), and (2) its inner substring is a palindrome (dp[i+1][j-1]) OR the substring has length <= 2 (base cases). We fill the table by iterating i from right to left and j from i to right, ensuring that when we check dp[i+1][j-1], it has already been computed. For lengths 1 and 2, we don't need to check the inner substring (j - i <= 2 handles this). As we fill the table, we track the longest palindrome found by comparing substring lengths. This approach reduces time complexity to O(n²) by avoiding redundant palindrome checks through memoization.
commonMistakes: Iterating in wrong order (must compute smaller substrings before larger ones)
Not handling base cases correctly (length 1 and 2 substrings)
Incorrect DP transition (forgetting to check outer characters match)
Off-by-one errors in substring extraction
Not initializing DP table properly (should be False by default)
solutions.whyItWorks: The DP approach works by building up from base cases (single characters and pairs) to larger substrings. The recurrence dp[i][j] = (s[i] == s[j]) AND (dp[i+1][j-1] OR j-i <= 2) correctly captures palindrome structure: outer characters must match, and either the inner part is a palindrome or there is no inner part (length <= 2). By iterating i backwards and j forwards from i, we ensure dependencies are satisfied. This avoids the O(n) palindrome check of the brute force approach by reusing previously computed results.
keyInsights: 2D DP table: dp[i][j] = true if s[i:j+1] is palindrome
Recurrence: s[i]==s[j] AND (j-i<=2 OR dp[i+1][j-1])
Iterate i backwards, j forwards to ensure dependencies computed
Base cases: length 1 (always palindrome) and length 2 (check if characters match)
O(n²) time by avoiding redundant palindrome checks

solutions.detailedExplanation: The expand-around-center approach treats each position (or pair of positions) as a potential palindrome center and expands outward. For each index i, we check two cases: (1) odd-length palindromes centered at i (start with l=r=i), and (2) even-length palindromes centered between i and i+1 (start with l=i, r=i+1). We expand outward (l--, r++) while the characters match and we're within bounds. During expansion, we track the longest palindrome found. This approach is more space-efficient than DP (O(1) extra space) while maintaining O(n²) time complexity. The key insight is that every palindrome has a center, which can be either a single character (odd length) or between two characters (even length).

Not checking bounds before accessing string indices (array out of bounds)
Updating result after expanding instead of during expansion (off-by-one errors)

Not handling single character strings correctly
solutions.whyItWorks: Every palindrome is symmetric around its center. By expanding from each possible center, we can find all palindromes. Odd-length palindromes have a single character center, while even-length palindromes have their center between two characters. Expanding outward while characters match naturally builds up the palindrome. We check n positions for odd-length and n-1 positions for even-length palindromes, and each expansion takes O(n) in the worst case, giving O(n²) total time. The space efficiency comes from not storing intermediate results - we just expand and update the maximum on the fly.

Two cases: odd-length (center at character) and even-length (center between characters)
Expand outward while characters match, updating maximum length
O(n²) time: n centers × O(n) expansion per center
O(1) extra space: no need to store intermediate results

solutions.name: Manacher's Algorithm
solutions.description: Use Manacher's Algorithm to find the longest palindrome in linear time. Transform the string by inserting separators to handle both odd and even length palindromes uniformly. Use previously computed palindrome information to avoid redundant checks, leveraging the symmetry property of palindromes.

python.code:
class Solution:
    def longestPalindrome(self, s: str) -> str:
        def manacher(s):
            t = '#' + '#'.join(s) + '#'
            n = len(t)
            p = [0] * n
            l, r = 0, 0
            for i in range(n):
                p[i] = min(r - i, p[l + (r - i)]) if i < r else 0
                while (i + p[i] + 1 < n and i - p[i] - 1 >= 0
                       and t[i + p[i] + 1] == t[i - p[i] - 1]):
                    p[i] += 1
                if i + p[i] > r:
                    l, r = i - p[i], i + p[i]
            return p

        p = manacher(s)
        resLen, center_idx = max((v, i) for i, v in enumerate(p))
        resIdx = (center_idx - resLen) // 2
        return s[resIdx : resIdx + resLen]

solutions.detailedExplanation: Manacher's Algorithm achieves linear time complexity by cleverly reusing information about previously found palindromes. First, we transform the input by inserting '#' between characters (e.g., 'aba' becomes '#a#b#a#'), which allows us to handle odd and even length palindromes uniformly. We maintain an array p where p[i] represents the radius of the longest palindrome centered at i in the transformed string. We also track the rightmost palindrome boundary (l, r). For each position i, we can leverage symmetry: if i is within a known palindrome, we can initialize p[i] using the mirror position's value. We then try to expand from this starting point. If we expand beyond the current rightmost boundary, we update it. This avoids redundant comparisons. After building the p array, we find the maximum radius and map it back to the original string. The algorithm is O(n) because each character is examined at most twice - once when expanding, once when using symmetry.
commonMistakes: Not transforming string correctly (missing '#' at boundaries or between chars)
Incorrect mirror calculation (should be l + (r - i), not r - i)
Not checking bounds before expanding (array access errors)
Incorrectly mapping back to original string indices
Not understanding why the algorithm is O(n) (each position examined limited times)
solutions.whyItWorks: Manacher's Algorithm exploits palindrome symmetry to avoid redundant work. When we know that position i is within a palindrome centered at c, we can use the palindrome radius at the mirror position (2*c - i) to initialize p[i]. This is valid because palindromes are symmetric. We still need to try expanding beyond this initial value, but we start from a better position. The key insight for O(n) complexity: each character is added to the rightmost boundary at most once (when we expand), and we examine it at most once when using symmetry. The transformation to add '#' is clever because it makes all palindromes have odd length in the transformed string, simplifying the algorithm.
keyInsights: Transform string with separators to handle odd/even lengths uniformly
Use symmetry within known palindromes to initialize new palindrome radius
Track rightmost palindrome boundary to enable symmetry optimization
Each character examined at most twice, giving O(n) complexity
Most sophisticated but optimal algorithm for palindrome substring problem
Requires understanding of amortized analysis to see O(n) time
